Subject: Partnership proposal for the Greenfields Digital Learning Programme

Thank you for meeting with our team on 16 October to discuss practical ways to improve access to digital skills in Greenfields. I am writing to propose a twelve-week community learning programme for adults who want to become more confident using computers and online services.

The programme will run at the Greenfields Community Centre twice each week. Participants will practise essential computer skills, safe internet use, email, document preparation and online job applications. Each group will have access to a facilitator, a prepared learning guide and shared computers. We plan to enrol 30 participants in the first group and will record attendance and progress throughout the course.

We would be pleased to work with Ubuntu Community Trust on participant referrals and venue access. Our team can provide the facilitator and course materials, while a contribution toward connectivity and equipment maintenance would help us keep the programme accessible. I have included a draft schedule and budget in the accompanying proposal.

Please let me know whether you would be available for a planning meeting during the week of 2 November. We can use that time to confirm responsibilities, agree on the participant referral process and review the final budget.

Thank you for your continued commitment to practical learning in our community. I look forward to the possibility of working together.

Yours sincerely,

Amina Ndlovu
Community Programmes Manager
Greenfields Learning Collective

html:
Community Digital Learning Programme

Programme outcomes report · January–September 2026
Prepared by the Greenfields Learning Collective

Executive Summary

This report reviews nine months of community digital skills training at Greenfields Community Centre. Three learning groups completed the programme, with 72 of 84 enrolled participants attending at least three quarters of the sessions. Learners reported greater confidence using email, preparing documents and searching for work online. The strongest results came from hands-on practice, patient facilitator support and lessons connected to everyday needs. The programme should continue with more open practice time, a simple device-lending arrangement and follow-up sessions after graduation.

1. Introduction

Digital services are now part of job seeking, communication and access to public information. Yet many adults have limited opportunities to practise using a computer with personal support. Greenfields Learning Collective established this programme to offer useful, welcoming instruction close to where people live. This report summarises participation, learning outcomes and practical improvements for the next programme cycle.

2. Approach

Participants attended two evening sessions each week for twelve weeks. Lessons covered computer basics, safe internet use, email, document formatting, online forms and job applications. Facilitators used demonstrations followed by individual practice. The team reviewed attendance registers, short skills activities completed at the beginning and end of each group, learner feedback forms and facilitator notes. These sources provide a useful programme picture, although they are not a controlled evaluation.

3. Findings

Participation and completion

Three groups enrolled 84 learners in total. Seventy-two attended at least 75 percent of sessions and 65 completed the final practical activity. Work schedules, transport costs and occasional connectivity problems were the most common reasons for missed sessions.

Practical confidence

At the end of the course, most participants could create and save a short document, send an email with an attachment and identify basic signs of a suspicious message. Learners especially valued repeating each task on their own device or on a shared computer after watching a demonstration. Facilitators observed that confidence grew when practice was not rushed and learners could ask questions without embarrassment.

Areas to improve

Some learners needed more time to practise keyboard and file-management skills before moving to online forms. Shared computers limited practice during busy sessions. A number of participants also requested a later session on spreadsheets and online applications.

4. Recommendations

  1. Keep the small-group teaching model and reserve at least half of each session for individual practice.
  2. Add an optional weekly open-lab hour for learners who need extra time or missed a class.
  3. Introduce a basic device and connectivity support plan with clear lending and return procedures.
  4. Offer a short follow-up workshop on spreadsheets and online job applications.
  5. Continue collecting attendance, practical task results and learner feedback in one simple review sheet.

5. Conclusion

The programme helped participants practise digital tasks that matter in daily life and work. Its results show the value of accessible local training that combines clear demonstrations with patient, repeated practice. Addressing access to devices and allowing more time for foundational skills will make the next cycle stronger.

Next Review

The programme team will confirm the next group schedule in November 2026 and review the recommendations with community partners before registration opens.

Project Proposal: Greenfields Digital Confidence Programme

Prepared for: Ubuntu Community Trust
Prepared by: Greenfields Learning Collective

Overview

Greenfields Learning Collective proposes a twelve-week digital skills programme for adults in the Greenfields community. The programme will help participants practise computer basics, online safety, email, document creation and online job applications in a supportive local setting.

Community Need

Residents have told local partners that they need more opportunities to practise everyday computer tasks with someone available to help. Limited access to devices and unfamiliarity with online forms can make job searches, communication and access to information harder. A small-group course at the community centre offers a practical, nearby starting point.

Objectives

  • Enrol and support one group of 30 adult learners.
  • Deliver two practical learning sessions each week for twelve weeks.
  • Enable learners to complete a basic document, send an email attachment and identify common online safety risks.
  • Track attendance, practical activities and participant feedback to guide improvements.

Scope and Delivery

The programme includes participant outreach, a short orientation, 24 facilitated sessions, printed lesson guides, shared computer access and a completion review. Lessons will use demonstrations followed by individual practice. Facilitators will adapt the pace to the group and provide optional open-lab time for learners who need additional support.

name: Academic paper
desc: A complete short paper with an abstract, argument and references
html:
Community-Based Digital Learning and Adult Confidence

Lerato Mokoena
Community Education Studies · Open Learning Institute
October 2026

Abstract

This paper considers how community-based adult learning can support confidence with everyday digital tasks. It argues that access to a device is important but does not, on its own, ensure that a learner feels able to use digital services. Confidence develops through relevant practice, supportive instruction and opportunities to repeat tasks without fear of embarrassment. A review of a small community learning programme illustrates how guided activities such as creating a document, sending an attachment and completing an online form can connect digital skills to learners’ immediate goals. The discussion draws on the capability approach, which emphasises people’s real opportunities to act, and on diffusion research, which highlights the role of communication and social context in the adoption of new practices. The paper concludes that local programmes should combine device access with patient facilitation, accessible materials and follow-up practice. These approaches cannot resolve every structural barrier, but they can make digital participation more achievable for adults who have had limited opportunities to learn.

Introduction

Many essential activities now involve digital tools, including finding work, communicating with organisations and accessing information. For adults who have not had regular access to computers, these activities can involve both technical and emotional barriers. A learner may understand a demonstration yet still hesitate when asked to complete the same task alone. Community learning programmes can respond by bringing instruction closer to participants and making practice part of the lesson rather than an optional extra.

Conceptual Context

The capability approach distinguishes access to resources from the real freedom to use those resources to pursue valued goals (Sen, 1999). A shared computer is therefore only one part of digital inclusion; learners also need time, support and relevant opportunities to practise. Diffusion of innovations research similarly shows that adoption is shaped by communication, experience and the social setting in which a new practice is introduced (Rogers, 2003). Together, these perspectives suggest that digital learning should be designed around people’s circumstances and goals.

Approach

This short discussion uses a descriptive review of a twelve-week community programme. Facilitator notes, attendance summaries and participant feedback were considered to identify common learning conditions. The review is illustrative rather than experimental: it does not establish that the programme alone caused changes in confidence, and its observations should not be generalised to every adult learning context.

Discussion

Three features appeared useful. First, lessons began with tasks participants recognised, such as sending an email or saving a document. This made the purpose of each skill clear. Second, demonstrations were followed by individual practice, allowing participants to repeat a task with support nearby. Third, the learning environment treated questions and mistakes as a normal part of practice. Participants often described feeling more comfortable when they could ask for help without slowing down a large class.

These observations point to a practical distinction between exposure and capability. Seeing a task performed can introduce a skill, but repeated use is more likely to help someone feel ready to act independently. Short follow-up sessions and access to devices between classes may therefore be as important as the initial course. Community programmes should also consider transport, connectivity, language and accessibility when planning participation.

Limitations

The programme was small and did not include a comparison group or long-term follow-up. Attendance and self-reported confidence provide useful feedback but cannot demonstrate lasting changes in digital participation. Further evaluation could follow learners several months after the course and include practical task observations alongside participant interviews.

Conclusion

Community-based digital learning can create a supportive route into everyday computer use when it combines relevant tasks, repeated practice and respectful facilitation. Device access remains necessary, but learners also need time and encouragement to turn access into practical confidence. Future programmes should evaluate these supports over time and adapt them to local needs.

References

Rogers, E. M. (2003). Diffusion of innovations (5th ed.). Free Press.

Sen, A. (1999). Development as freedom. Oxford University Press.

name: Thesis outline
html:
Beyond Access: Adult Digital Learning in Community Settings

Research outline by Lerato Mokoena
Master of Community Education · Open Learning Institute
Research proposal, 2026

Research Problem

Community digital skills courses are often assessed by enrolment and attendance, although these measures do not show whether learners feel able to use digital tools independently after training. This study will explore how adult learners describe the conditions that help or hinder their confidence during community-based digital learning.

Research Question

How do adult learners experience and describe the support that helps them develop confidence with everyday digital tasks in a community learning programme?

Chapter 1 — Introduction

This chapter will introduce the study context, define the research problem and explain why adult digital learning matters to community participation. It will state the research question, objectives and key terms, then describe the scope and limitations of the project. The chapter will clarify that the study focuses on learner experience rather than measuring the performance of a particular device or software product.

Chapter 2 — Literature Review

The literature review will examine digital inclusion, adult learning, learner confidence and community education. It will consider the difference between having access to technology and having a meaningful opportunity to use it. The chapter will use the capability approach and research on the adoption of new practices as guiding perspectives, while noting that local context shapes how these ideas apply.

Chapter 3 — Methodology

The study will use a qualitative case-study design at one community learning centre. Approximately 12–15 adult learners who have attended a digital skills course will be invited to participate in semi-structured interviews. With consent, the researcher will also review lesson materials and facilitator reflections. Interview notes will be coded thematically to identify recurring experiences related to practice time, facilitator support, access to devices and perceived progress.

Chapter 4 — Findings and Discussion

This chapter will present themes from the interviews and relate them to the research question. Possible areas of discussion include the role of repeated practice, the effect of peer support, challenges caused by connectivity or transport, and the kinds of tasks learners find most useful. The final themes will be based on the collected data rather than decided in advance.

Chapter 5 — Conclusion and Recommendations

The final chapter will summarise the study’s contribution, explain its limitations and offer practical recommendations for community learning programmes. Recommendations will be grounded in participant accounts and may address lesson pacing, open practice sessions, accessible materials and follow-up support.

Ethics and Work Plan

Participation will be voluntary. Participants will receive a clear explanation of the study, provide informed consent and be able to withdraw without giving a reason. Names and identifying details will be removed from the final report. The proposed work plan is: literature review in November 2026; ethics and recruitment in December 2026; interviews in January and February 2027; analysis in March 2027; and final writing in April 2027.

Indicative References

Rogers, E. M. (2003). Diffusion of innovations (5th ed.). Free Press.

Sen, A. (1999). Development as freedom. Oxford University Press.

Welcome to our October update. This issue celebrates the learners and volunteers who make community education possible, shares dates for the next digital skills group and offers a few practical ways to keep learning between sessions.

Top Story: Learners Put New Digital Skills to Work

Sixty-five participants completed the Greenfields digital learning programme this year. During the final session, learners prepared a short document, saved it to a folder and sent it by email. For many, the proudest moment was completing each step independently after weeks of practice. Facilitators say the group’s patience with one another helped make the room a place where questions were welcome.

The next twelve-week group begins on 9 November at Greenfields Community Centre. Sessions will run on Monday and Wednesday evenings. Registration is open until 4 November, and places are limited so that facilitators can provide individual support.

Volunteer Spotlight

Kabelo Dlamini has volunteered as a technology support assistant throughout the year. He tests the computers before each course, helps learners practise file management and patiently troubleshoots connection problems. Kabelo says his favourite part is watching someone go from “I cannot do this” to completing the task and showing a neighbour how it works.

Try This at Home

Practise creating a folder with a name you will remember. Save one document inside it, close the document and open it again from the folder. Repeating a small task is a useful way to build confidence. If you use a shared device, remember to sign out of personal accounts when you finish.

name: Blog post
desc: A complete article with practical advice and a clear conclusion
html:
Small Practice, Big Progress: Building Digital Confidence One Task at a Time

Greenfields Learning Collective · 24 October 2026 · 5 minute read

Learning to use a computer can feel like a big challenge when every button seems unfamiliar. The good news is that digital confidence rarely arrives all at once. It grows through small, useful tasks repeated in a supportive setting.

Start with a task that matters to you

Choose something you would like to do, such as writing a short letter, sending an email or searching for a job listing. A clear purpose makes it easier to understand why a tool is useful. It also gives you a way to notice your progress: the task that once needed help may soon feel familiar.

Repeat the steps, not just the demonstration

Watching someone else complete a task can introduce the steps, but confidence comes from trying them yourself. Create a document, save it, close it and find it again. Practise attaching a file to an email. If you make a mistake, pause and try again. Repetition turns a sequence of clicks into a routine you can remember.

“The best way to learn a digital task is to practise it for a reason that matters in your own life.”

Ask questions and learn with others

There is no age limit on learning technology, and asking for help is part of the process. A patient facilitator or fellow learner can make an unfamiliar task feel manageable. Explaining a step to someone else can also help you remember it yourself.

Keep your practice safe

Use strong, unique passwords and avoid sharing them. Before opening a link or attachment, check whether you recognise the sender and expected the message. On a shared computer, sign out of personal accounts when you finish. If something feels suspicious, ask someone you trust before responding.

Make progress visible

Keep a short list of tasks you can now complete. Add to it when you create your first saved document, send an attachment or fill out an online form. Small milestones show how far you have come and help you decide what to practise next.

Take the next step

Pick one practical task and practise it this week. Start slowly, repeat the steps and ask questions when you need support. Digital confidence is built one useful task at a time—and every new skill gives you another way to take part.

Join the conversation: What digital task would you most like to feel confident doing? Share your idea with the Greenfields Learning Collective at hello@greenfields.example.
